10360: To manipulate something or someone means to handle or control it skillfully and with clear intention — either physically (an object) or psychologically (a person or situation). The two key ingredients are always present: skill/cleverness and a goal you're working toward.

Meaning 1 — Physical / Technical (Neutral)

To physically handle, move, or operate something with care, precision, and skill — usually with your hands or with tools.

Examples:

  • A surgeon manipulates tiny instruments inside the body during a delicate operation.
  • A chiropractor manipulates the patient's spine to relieve pain.
  • The pilot manipulates the aircraft's controls to change direction.
  • A graphic designer manipulates an image on a computer to change its colors and shape.
  • A puppeteer manipulates strings to make the puppet walk and dance.

In this sense, the word carries no negative judgment at all. It simply describes skillful, intentional physical control. Think of it as meaning: "to handle something with expert care."

Meaning 2 — Psychological / Social (Negative)

To cleverly influence or control a person — or a situation — in an indirect, dishonest, or unfair way to get what you want, often without the other person fully realizing what is happening to them.

This is by far the most common everyday use of the word, and it almost always has a strongly negative meaning.

Examples:

  • He manipulated her into lending him money by pretending to be seriously ill.
  • The politician manipulated public opinion by selectively sharing only facts that supported his side.
  • She felt deeply manipulated when she discovered he had been making her feel guilty on purpose, just to control her behavior.
  • The company manipulated its financial records to hide how much money it had actually lost.
The Crucial Difference Between the Two Meanings

ContextToneExample

When "manipulate" is used about physical objects, tools, machines, or body parts, the word feels completely neutral — even professional.

When "manipulate" is used about people, emotions, or information, the word almost always feels negative — implying deception, hidden motives, and unfair control.

Data and statistics sit in an interesting middle ground. You can "manipulate data" in a neutral sense (process or arrange it), but in everyday speech, "manipulate data/figures/statistics" almost always means to distort or falsify them dishonestly.
What Makes Manipulation Different from Simple Force or Pressure?

This is important. Manipulation is subtle. A manipulator does not usually threaten you openly or force you directly. Instead, they:

  • Work quietly through your emotions — especially guilt, fear, love, pity, or insecurity.
  • Make you feel as if you are choosing freely, when in reality they are quietly steering your choices.
  • Hide their true intentions and make their actions look innocent or even kind.

This is what makes manipulation particularly harmful and difficult to detect. The person being manipulated often doesn't notice it while it's happening. When they do eventually realize it, they typically feel betrayed, used, and foolish.

A simple bully who says "Give me your lunch or I'll hit you" is using force. A manipulator who says "You're such a good friend — I know you'd never let me go hungry" while playing on your kindness is manipulating. The outcome may be the same (you give away your lunch), but the method is completely different.

Here are the most natural ways "manipulate" appears in sentences:

  • Manipulate someone → He manipulated everyone around him.
  • Manipulate someone into doing something → She manipulated him into resigning.
  • Manipulate someone's feelings/emotions → He manipulated her emotions to make her stay.
  • Manipulate a situation → She cleverly manipulated the situation to her advantage.
  • Manipulate data / figures / statistics / records → They manipulated the data to get the result they wanted.
  • Manipulate public opinion / the media → The regime manipulated the media to control what citizens believed.
  • Manipulate a joint / limb / spine (medical) → The therapist gently manipulated his injured shoulder.
  • Manipulate controls / instruments (technical) → She manipulated the robotic arm with great precision.

• Physical objects or tools → Neutral to positive (skillful).
  • People or emotions → Strongly negative (dishonest, exploitative).
  • Data, statistics, or records → Almost always negative (falsified or distorted).

In the psychological/social sense (negative):
exploit, deceive, scheme, trick, coerce, use, con, pull strings, play someone

In the physical/technical sense (neutral):
handle, operate, control, maneuver, wield, work
A Quick Way to Remember It

Think of a puppet master. With one hand, they manipulate the puppet's strings — that's the physical, skillful sense. Now imagine a person who controls you the same way — pulling invisible strings, making you act and feel the way they want, without you even seeing the strings. That's the psychological sense.

"Manipulate" always means skilled, intentional control. The question is whether you're controlling an object (fine) or a person (almost always wrong).
10361:
Manipulation is the act of controlling, influencing, or handling something or someone — but how it is done is what gives the word its meaning.

The word is used in two broad ways: a neutral/technical sense and a negative/psychological sense. Most of the time in everyday life, when people say "manipulation," they mean the second one. But a complete understanding requires knowing both.

In certain professional or technical contexts, manipulation simply means the skillful handling or operation of something — usually with the hands or through a system.

Examples:

  • A surgeon performs the manipulation of delicate instruments during an operation — meaning careful, precise physical handling.
  • A physiotherapist uses spinal manipulation to correct alignment — meaning controlled movement of the body.
  • A photographer does image manipulation — meaning altering or editing a photo.
  • A programmer does data manipulation — meaning processing or changing data in a system.

In these uses, the word carries no moral judgment. It just means: skilled, deliberate handling of something.
2. The Negative, Psychological Sense (The Main Meaning)

This is the sense most people mean, and it is far more important to understand deeply.

Psychological manipulation is the act of controlling or influencing a person's thoughts, feelings, or actions through dishonest, indirect, or unfair means — often for the manipulator's own benefit, and usually in a way that the other person doesn't fully realize is happening.

What Makes Something "Manipulation" and Not Just Influence?

This is the key question. People influence each other all the time — through advice, arguments, advertising, teaching. Not all of it is manipulation. So what separates manipulation from normal influence?

Three things must typically be present:

1. Hidden or dishonest intent
The manipulator doesn't reveal their true goal. They pretend to care about you, or they frame things in a misleading way, so that you don't realize you're being steered.

2. Bypassing your rational thinking
Instead of giving you honest information and letting you decide freely, the manipulator targets your emotions, fears, insecurities, desires, or psychological weaknesses. They get you to act not through reason, but through pressure or distortion.

3. The benefit flows to the manipulator, often at your expense
Even when it's disguised as being "for your own good," manipulation ultimately serves the manipulator's agenda — not necessarily yours.

Manipulation vs. Persuasion — A Critical Distinction

Many learners confuse manipulation with persuasion. Here is the difference:

Persuasion is honest. A person who persuades you gives you real arguments, truthful evidence, and their genuine point of view. You understand what they want and why. Your decision remains free and informed.

Manipulation is dishonest. A person who manipulates you distorts information, plays on your emotions unfairly, or hides their true motives. Your decision is not truly free — it has been engineered without your full awareness.

An example:

  • Persuasion: "I think you should invest in this business. Here are the real risks and rewards. Think it over."
  • Manipulation: "I know money is tight for you. Think about what your family would say if you missed this once-in-a-lifetime chance. Everyone else is already in."

The second example works by creating fear, guilt, and false urgency — not by giving you true information.

Common Forms of Psychological Manipulation

Manipulation is not one single act. It shows up in many patterns:

Guilt-tripping: Making someone feel responsible for the manipulator's pain or unhappiness to get a desired outcome. "After everything I've done for you, you can't do this one thing?"

Gaslighting: Making a person doubt their own memory, perception, or sanity. "That never happened. You're imagining things. You're too sensitive." This is a particularly destructive form.

Emotional blackmail: Using fear, obligation, or guilt to force a decision. "If you really loved me, you wouldn't question this."

Flattery with a hidden motive: Giving exaggerated praise not out of genuine appreciation but to put you in a position where you feel obligated to return the favor.

Playing the victim: Exaggerating or faking helplessness or suffering to gain sympathy and control others' behavior.

False urgency: Creating artificial pressure so you act quickly before you have time to think clearly. "This offer expires tonight — you must decide now."

Selective information: Sharing only the facts that support what the manipulator wants, hiding the rest.

Shifting goalposts: Constantly changing the conditions or expectations so the other person can never "win" or feel secure without constantly complying.

Manipulation in Different Contexts

Manipulation doesn't only happen in personal relationships. It appears across many areas of life:

In relationships: A partner, family member, or friend who controls through guilt, emotional pressure, or distorted reality.

In the workplace: A manager or colleague who takes credit for others' work, pits teammates against each other, or uses favoritism and fear to maintain control.

In politics: Politicians or public figures who distort facts, appeal to irrational fears, or use propaganda to steer public opinion.

In advertising and media: Techniques designed to make you feel insecure, envious, or afraid so that you buy a product or accept an idea without thinking critically.

In finance: Market manipulation is a specific legal term for illegally influencing stock prices or financial markets through deceptive trading.

The Harm of Manipulation

Understanding why manipulation is considered wrong is just as important as knowing what it is.

When someone is manipulated, their ability to make free, informed decisions is taken away from them — even if they don't realize it. This is a violation of their autonomy (their right to decide their own path based on accurate information and their own genuine values).

Manipulation also erodes trust. When people discover they've been manipulated, the relationship — personal, professional, or public — is damaged, sometimes irreparably. It creates an environment where people are always on guard and can no longer take things at face value.

Over time, being manipulated repeatedly can damage a person's self-confidence, their ability to trust their own judgment, and their mental health.

Is Manipulation Always Intentional?

Mostly, yes — but not always completely conscious. Some people have learned manipulative patterns from childhood or from environments where manipulation was the norm, and they use these patterns without full awareness. This doesn't make the manipulation harmless or acceptable, but it adds nuance: not every manipulator is a calculated, scheming villain. Some genuinely don't realize how their behavior affects others.

That said, the most harmful forms of manipulation — gaslighting, emotional blackmail, deliberate deception — are typically very conscious and calculated.

How to Spot Manipulation

Since manipulation often works by hiding itself, here are signals worth noticing:

  • You frequently feel guilty, afraid, or confused after interacting with someone, but you can't quite explain why.
  • Someone's version of events keeps shifting in their favor.
  • You feel pressured to decide quickly, before you've had time to think.
  • Your own perceptions and memories are regularly questioned or denied.
  • Compliments feel like they come with strings attached.
  • You feel like you can never do enough to satisfy someone, yet you keep trying harder.

Manipulation (noun) means:

  1. In technical or neutral contexts: the skillful, controlled handling of something physical or digital.
  2. In its primary, everyday meaning: the act of controlling or influencing a person through dishonest, indirect, or unfair means — bypassing their rational thinking, exploiting their emotions or vulnerabilities, and serving the manipulator's hidden agenda, often without the other person's awareness.

The word lives at the intersection of power, deception, and psychology. When you see it used, it almost always signals that someone's free will and honest understanding have been compromised — and that is precisely why manipulation is universally considered a harmful and unethical act.
10362: Manna is a word that carries three connected meanings: a miraculous food from the Bible, a real natural substance found in certain plants, and a figurative expression for any unexpected, life-saving gift or blessing. All three uses of the word are active in the English language today, and understanding all three will give you complete command of the word.

This is the original and most well-known meaning of manna. In the Bible, specifically in the book of Exodus, the Israelites were wandering through the desert after escaping slavery in Egypt. They had no food and were starving. Then, each morning, when the dew on the ground dried up, a mysterious white, flaky substance was left behind on the desert floor — almost like frost or thin flakes of bread. God had sent this food to keep the Israelites alive. The people called it manna.

Here is what the Bible tells us about what manna was like:

  • It was white and small, like tiny seeds or like frost on the ground.
  • It tasted sweet, like bread made with honey.
  • It appeared every single morning, six days a week, reliably and without fail.
  • Each person was supposed to collect only enough for one day. If anyone got greedy and collected extra to save for the next day, it would rot overnight and become full of worms.
  • The only exception was the day before the Sabbath (the Jewish day of rest on Saturday). On that day, they were allowed to collect double the amount, and miraculously, it would not rot overnight.
  • This went on for forty years, the entire time the Israelites were wandering in the desert. The moment they crossed into the Promised Land (Canaan) and had access to regular food, the manna stopped appearing.
  • A small portion of manna was preserved in a golden jar and kept inside the Ark of the Covenant as a permanent reminder of God's provision.

In short, manna in this original biblical sense means: a miraculous food sent directly from God to sustain human life in a time of desperate need. It was not hunted, grown, or earned. It simply arrived. This is why it became so powerful as a symbol.

Manna is not only a religious or symbolic word. It also refers to a real, physical substance found in nature.

Certain plants and trees — most famously a tree called the manna ash, common in Mediterranean regions — produce a sweet, sugary liquid that oozes out through the bark (especially when the bark is cut). When this liquid is exposed to air, it dries and hardens into light, crumbly, whitish flakes or lumps. This hardened sugary substance is called manna.

Some important facts about this natural manna:

  • It is very sweet and contains a type of natural sugar.
  • It has been used for centuries as a mild laxative (a medicine that helps with digestion and bowel movement). It is gentle enough to be given to children.
  • It is also found in other plants, such as tamarisk trees, which produce a similar sweet secretion.
  • Some historians and scientists have actually suggested that the biblical manna the Israelites ate may have been inspired by, or even been, this kind of natural plant secretion — but that remains a topic of scholarly debate.

So when you see the word "manna" in a botanical, scientific, or medical context, it refers to this sweet, hardened plant secretion.
Meaning 3: Figurative — An Unexpected Gift or Blessing

This is the meaning you will most commonly encounter in everyday English. Because of its powerful biblical origin, the word "manna" has become a widely used figurative expression for anything that:

  • Arrives unexpectedly
  • Is desperately needed
  • Feels like a gift or stroke of great luck
  • Provides relief, nourishment, or salvation at just the right moment

The most common phrase you will hear is "manna from heaven." It means an unexpected windfall, gift, or benefit that arrives at a moment when you really needed it — as if it fell from the sky, just like the biblical manna did.

Examples of how people use it:

  • "After months of drought, the rain that finally fell was manna from heaven for the farmers."
  • "The donation we received was absolute manna from heaven — we were about to shut the charity down."
  • "For a student who hadn't eaten all day, that free pizza was manna."

You can also use it without the phrase "from heaven," simply calling something "manna" to mean it was a godsend or an extraordinary blessing. The figurative use always carries the idea that the good thing arrived without you having to work directly for it, almost as if it was granted to you by a higher power or by fate.

The three meanings are not separate or unrelated. They flow naturally from one to the next:

The real plant substance (sweet, white, nourishing, appears in the wild) is where the word began. The biblical story took that image and elevated it into something miraculous and divine. And the figurative use borrowed the feeling of the biblical story — the sense of helplessness, the desperation, and then the sudden, unearned relief — and applied it to any situation in modern life that creates that same feeling.

SenseWhat it means

To put it plainly:

  • Literal/Biblical: The miraculous food God sent to the Israelites in the desert every morning for forty years — white, sweet, and unexplainable.
  • Natural/Scientific: A real sweet, sugary substance secreted by certain trees like the manna ash, used historically as food and medicine.
  • Figurative: Any unexpected, desperately needed gift, benefit, or blessing that feels like it came from nowhere — often used in the phrase "manna from heaven."

Master these three senses and you will understand every use of the word "manna" you will ever encounter.
10363: A mannequin is a full-sized, three-dimensional model shaped like a human body. It is not alive — it is an artificial, inanimate object, typically made of materials like plastic, fiberglass, or foam. The key purpose of a mannequin is simple: to represent the human figure so that something — most often clothing — can be placed on it and displayed.
The Main Meaning: A Display Dummy

When you walk past a clothing store and see a rigid, human-shaped figure wearing an outfit in the shop window or on the store floor, that figure is a mannequin.

Stores use mannequins because they allow customers to see how a piece of clothing — a dress, a suit, a jacket — actually looks when it is worn on a body, rather than just folded on a shelf. A mannequin gives the garment shape, form, and a sense of life. It is, essentially, a stand-in for a real human body.

Mannequins can be:

  • Realistic — with detailed facial features, skin tones, hair, and lifelike body proportions, meant to closely resemble real people.
  • Abstract or stylized — featureless, plain white or grey, sometimes with no head or hands, representing the body shape in a simplified, artistic way.

They come in versions representing men, women, and children, and in a range of body shapes and sizes. Many modern mannequins reflect more diverse body types, including plus-sized figures.

A mannequin is also not always a complete body. You will frequently see:

  • Torso mannequins — showing only the upper body (chest, shoulders, arms), used for displaying shirts, jackets, and tops.
  • Lower-body mannequins — showing only the hips and legs, used for trousers, skirts, and leggings.
  • Bust forms — showing only the chest area, used for displaying jewellery, scarves, or necklines.
  • Head mannequins — used to display hats, glasses, wigs, and headwear.
A Second Meaning: A Human Fashion Model (Older Usage)

Historically, and still occasionally in formal or fashion-industry contexts, the word mannequin was used to refer to a real, living person — a human being employed to wear and show off clothing for buyers, designers, or customers. In today's language, we almost always call such a person a model instead. The human sense of the word is now largely old-fashioned or rare in everyday English, but you may still encounter it in older texts or fashion writing.

Beyond clothing retail, the word "mannequin" appears in a few other specific contexts:

  • Artist's mannequin (also called a lay figure or posable mannequin): A small, jointed wooden or plastic figure, shaped like a human, used by painters, illustrators, and sculptors. It can be bent and positioned into different poses, helping the artist study how a human body looks in a particular stance or angle. These are typically much smaller than life-sized — often around 20–30 cm tall.
  • Medical or training mannequins: Life-sized, human-shaped models used for training purposes — for example, CPR practice mannequins, on which medical students or first-aid learners practice chest compressions and resuscitation techniques.
  • Tailor's dress form: Sometimes loosely called a mannequin, this is a torso-shaped stand used by tailors and dressmakers to fit, pin, and construct garments while they are being made. It mimics the shape of the human upper body so clothing can be shaped accurately.
  • Crash test mannequins (called "crash test dummies"): These are highly engineered, human-shaped figures used in vehicle safety testing. Cars are crashed, and these dummies measure the impact on a human-like body. While technically called "dummies," they are essentially a specialised form of mannequin.
The Feeling and Associations of the Word

Mannequins are often noted for their uncanny quality — they look human but are obviously not. This "almost-but-not-quite-human" appearance makes them a common image in art, literature, and film when writers or directors want to evoke feelings of eeriness, stillness, artificiality, or lifelessness. A room full of mannequins can feel unsettling precisely because they mimic human form without possessing any of its warmth or movement.

• The store had dressed several mannequins in its new winter collection and placed them near the entrance.
  • She adjusted the scarf on the mannequin so that it draped naturally over the shoulder.
  • The art student positioned the small wooden mannequin with one arm raised so he could sketch the pose accurately.
  • The emergency room trainees practised on a mannequin before treating real patients.

A mannequin is, at its most essential, a human-shaped model used as a substitute for a real body — most famously to display clothing in shops, but also used by artists for reference, by tailors to fit garments, and by trainers to practise life-saving skills. It is always inanimate, always shaped like a person (or part of a person), and always serving the function of representing the human form for a practical purpose.
10364:
Imagine you are watching someone act in a movie. The actor is so focused on how they are performing — the dramatic pauses, the exaggerated gestures, the overly theatrical voice — that you stop believing in the character. You start watching the performance itself instead of feeling the story. That experience is what the word mannered captures.

Mannered means artificially stylized or affected — when something (or someone) is so self-consciously performed, so deliberately styled, that it feels unnatural, forced, and exaggerated rather than genuine and spontaneous.
The Word Has Two Distinct Uses

Use 1: Standing Alone — The Primary Meaning

When "mannered" stands by itself (not attached to another word), it describes something or someone that feels overly calculated, theatrical, or artificial in style or behavior. The "manner" has become so exaggerated that it stops looking real and starts looking like a performance of itself.

Think of it on a simple scale:

Natural → Stylish → Mannered

The moment a style crosses from "refined and distinctive" into "so elaborate and self-conscious that it feels fake" — that's when we call it mannered.

This is a word used mainly in contexts like art, writing, film, music, and personal behavior.

Use 2: Combined with Another Word — The Compound Form

"Mannered" is also the second half of compound adjectives, where it simply means having manners of a particular kind:

  • Well-mannered → having good manners
  • Ill-mannered → having bad manners
  • Mild-mannered → having a quiet, gentle manner
  • Bad-mannered → behaving rudely

In this use, "mannered" on its own carries very little meaning — it needs that first part (well-, ill-, mild-) to make sense. This use is relatively straightforward.

The more interesting, nuanced, and frequently tested meaning is Use 1, so let's go deep on that.
Going Deep: What "Mannered" Really Means When Used Alone

The key insight is this: mannerisms are fine in small doses, but when they take over, they become "mannered."

Every artist, writer, speaker, or person has their own natural tendencies — the way they phrase things, move, express emotion. Those tendencies are just style. But when a person becomes so aware of their own style that they start performing it deliberately and exaggeratedly, it stops being authentic. The style is no longer serving the work or the moment — the style is the point. That's when critics and observers use the word "mannered."

It carries a slightly negative or critical tone. Calling something "mannered" is almost always a mild criticism — a suggestion that it has traded authenticity for self-conscious stylishness.

In Acting:
An actor who pauses dramatically before every line, raises their eyebrows precisely the same way in every emotional scene, and speaks with a perfectly controlled, theatrical voice might be called a mannered actor. You can see them trying to act, rather than just being in the moment. Compare this to an actor who makes you forget they're performing at all — that actor is the opposite of mannered.

In Writing:
A mannered writing style is one where the author is so absorbed in sounding sophisticated or literary that the writing draws attention to itself rather than to the story or ideas. Extremely long, elaborate sentences piled with unusual words, where you keep thinking "the author is showing off" instead of just reading — that's mannered prose.

In Music or Art:
A musician whose every note is so precisely controlled and stylistically exaggerated that the music feels emotionally cold and calculated. A painter whose brushwork is so self-consciously detailed and theatrical that the painting feels more like a technical display than an expression of feeling.

In Personal Behavior:
A person who speaks in an unusually formal, theatrical way in ordinary conversation — carefully enunciating every word, making sweeping gestures, adopting poses — can be described as having a mannered way of speaking or behaving. It feels like they are performing rather than just talking.

When something is mannered, the general feeling is:

  • It is trying too hard.
  • You are more aware of the style than the substance.
  • It has sacrificed naturalness in favour of deliberate effect.
  • There is a kind of stiffness or coldness underneath all the elaborate surface.
  • It feels rehearsed rather than alive.

A good test: if you catch yourself thinking "this person/artist/writer seems very conscious of how they look/sound right now," the word "mannered" probably applies.

It does not simply mean having a style. Every good artist or writer has a style, and that's a compliment. "Mannered" kicks in only when the style becomes so exaggerated and self-conscious that it overshadows everything else.

It is also not the same as bad. Something can be mannered but still technically brilliant — the criticism is specifically about the artificial, over-stylized quality, not about skill or quality in general. Critics might say, "it's beautifully crafted but rather mannered," meaning: impressive, but the self-consciousness gets in the way.

Core meaning (standalone):Artificially stylized; excessively self-conscious in style or behavior; affected; the manner is so deliberate and exaggerated it no longer feels natural
Core meaning (combined):Having a certain kind of manners (well-mannered, ill-mannered, mild-mannered)
Tone:Mildly critical when used alone
Used for:People, writing, acting, art, music, speech, behavior
The key test:Does the style call attention to itself at the expense of naturalness? If yes → mannered

If you remember just one thing: mannered means so deliberately and self-consciously styled that it no longer feels genuine — the style is performing itself, rather than serving anything real.
10365: The word mannerism has two major layers of meaning. One is about everyday human behavior, and the other is about art and creative style.
Meaning 1: A distinctive personal habit or quirk

At its most everyday level, a mannerism is a small, repeated habit that is so characteristic of a particular person that it becomes recognizable as theirs. It is not just any habit — it is a distinctive one. A behavioral fingerprint, of sorts.

These can show up in how someone:

  • Moves or gestures — always tapping their pen while thinking, twirling their hair, or shrugging one specific shoulder
  • Speaks — always starting sentences with "Look...", always saying "you know what I mean?" after every point, or dropping their voice to nearly a whisper when excited
  • Carries themselves — always tilting their head when confused, raising one eyebrow when skeptical, or clicking their tongue before disagreeing

The key thing about a mannerism is that it is repeated and recognizable. It is not a one-off thing. It is the sort of behavior that, once you notice it in someone, you cannot stop noticing.

Is a mannerism good, bad, or neutral?

Technically neutral — it simply means a characteristic personal habit. However, in everyday speech, the word carries a very slight negative lean. When someone says "he has some odd mannerisms," it usually suggests the habits are a little strange, irritating, or at least worth pointing out. A charming personal quirk might simply be called a "quirk" — when the word "mannerism" is used, it often implies the habit is a bit excessive or noticeable in a way that is slightly off-putting.

Notice also that the plural — mannerisms — is extremely common. People rarely have just one. You will often hear: "She has so many mannerisms," or "The actor captured the character's mannerisms perfectly."
Meaning 2: An exaggerated or artificial stylistic habit in art, writing, or performance

In the world of creative work — writing, painting, acting, filmmaking, music — a mannerism refers to a stylistic habit that has become so overused or exaggerated that it starts to feel hollow, mechanical, or self-conscious.

Here is how to think about it:

Every creative person develops a style. A great novelist might use short, punchy sentences. A filmmaker might love slow, lingering close-ups. A painter might always choose unusual, moody colors. When these choices feel genuine and serve the work well, they are simply called style.

But when those same choices are repeated so mechanically that they no longer serve the work — when the creator seems to be just going through their stylistic motions — they become mannerisms. They stop being tools and start being crutches.

Examples:

  • A novelist who uses fragmented, poetic sentences in every scene, even action scenes that call for urgency and speed — the technique has become a mannerism
  • An actor who pauses dramatically before every important line — not because the scene demands it, but because it is his "signature move" — that pause is a mannerism
  • A director who uses a slow-motion shot in nearly every climactic moment, until the audience starts predicting it rather than feeling it — that is a mannerism

The central problem with a mannerism in this sense is that it draws attention to itself rather than to the work. The audience notices the trick instead of feeling the story. Critics often use this word as a gentle form of disapproval: "The film is beautifully shot, but the director's mannerisms begin to distract in the second half."
Meaning 3: Mannerism (with a capital M) — A specific art movement

When the word is written with a capital M, it refers to a specific and well-defined movement in European art history, roughly from the 1520s through to around 1600 — sitting between the High Renaissance and the period known as the Baroque.

Artists in this movement deliberately pulled away from the calm, natural, balanced ideals of the Renaissance (think Leonardo da Vinci or Raphael). Instead, they leaned into something more deliberately strange, sophisticated, and artificial — almost as if they were showing off how clever and skilled they were.

Characteristics of Mannerist art include:

  • Human figures that are unnaturally elongated, stretched, and gracefully twisted into complex poses
  • Crowded, busy compositions that feel tense rather than serene
  • Unusual, sometimes eerie colors — cool blues, acid yellows, strange flesh tones
  • Lighting that does not follow natural logic
  • A general sense of elegance that feels studied and deliberate rather than effortless

Famous Mannerist artists include El Greco (known for his dramatically elongated, swirling religious figures), Pontormo, Bronzino, and Parmigianino. Looking at their work, you instantly sense that something is deliberately "off" compared to the more natural look of Renaissance art — and that is entirely intentional.

Mannerism, as an art movement, is essentially style celebrated for its own sake. It is sophisticated, self-aware, and technically brilliant — but it prioritizes ingenuity and elegance over naturalism and simplicity.
The thread that ties all three meanings together

Across all three uses of the word, the common idea is this: a recognizable, repeated pattern that is distinctive, often slightly exaggerated, and sometimes self-conscious.

ContextWhat "mannerism" means
  • In everyday life, a mannerism is a distinctive behavioral habit tied to a specific person.
  • In creative work, a mannerism is a stylistic habit that has been overused to the point of feeling artificial or automatic.
  • In art history, Mannerism (capital M) is a whole movement built on deliberate stylization, sophistication, and artificiality.

The word mannered (the adjective form) means having obvious, conspicuous, or affected mannerisms — often used critically. "His acting felt overly mannered" means the performance felt artificial and full of self-conscious stylistic tricks.

And affected is a word you will often see paired with mannerism. An affected mannerism is one that seems put-on or fake — not a genuine natural habit, but something someone has consciously adopted to appear a certain way, which has then hardened into an unconscious tic.
10366:
"Manqué" describes a person who had the potential, the desire, or the inner spirit to become something — but never actually became it. It points to an identity that could have been, and wasn't.

The simplest way to hold it in your mind: a [something] manqué is a person who was meant to be a [something], but life went differently.

A poet manqué is not a poet. They are someone who, deep down, had the makings of a poet — the sensitivity, the vision, the longing — but ended up being, say, an insurance clerk instead. The poetry never happened. Yet you can see traces of it in them.
What Makes It Precise (and Different from Just "Failed")

This is where the word gets interesting, and where most simple definitions fall short.

"Manqué" is not simply a synonym for "failed" or "unsuccessful." The distinction matters.

A failed poet tried to be a poet and didn't succeed. There's an active attempt that went wrong.

A poet manqué may never have seriously attempted poetry at all. They may have become an engineer at 22 and stayed one their whole life. But the poetic nature was always there, suppressed or sidelined. The word is about unrealized potential and unfulfilled identity, not just a botched attempt.

So the failure "manqué" describes is softer and more wistful than outright failure. It's more like: "this person had it in them, and the world — or circumstance, or duty, or fear — just never let it out."

There's also something that "manqué" captures that "failed" doesn't: the idea that the person themselves is somehow marked by this unfulfilled identity. A poet manqué doesn't just happen to have never written poetry. You can sense it about them. They speak in metaphors. They notice light differently. The unlived life clings to them.

Here is a strict rule you must know: "manqué" always comes after the noun it describes, not before it.

You say: "a poet manqué" ✔

You do not say: "a manqué poet" ✘

This is unusual for English adjectives, which normally sit before their noun ("a tall man," "a broken clock"). "Manqué" borrows French grammar here, and the convention has been preserved in English. Every single example you will ever read places the word after the noun.

"Manqué" is not a harsh or cruel word. It doesn't mock the person. Its tone sits somewhere between wistful, ironic, and affectionate — and sometimes all three at once.

When you call someone "a diplomat manqué," you might be gently teasing them about their natural talent for smoothing things over in conversation, while also acknowledging that they never pursued diplomacy. There's a rueful quality to it — a quiet "what might have been."

It can be applied to others or to oneself. A person might say, "I'm a musician manqué — I took up law to please my parents and never looked back, though I've regretted it." There's honesty and a little sadness in that, but not bitterness.

"Manqué" describes people, specifically in reference to a role, profession, vocation, or identity they did not fulfill. The noun before it is always the thing they could have been or might have been.

Common examples in real usage:

  • A writer manqué — someone with a writer's sensibility who never wrote.
  • An actor manqué — someone with natural performance ability who ended up in a completely different field.
  • A revolutionary manqué — someone with the fire and convictions of a revolutionary who never got the chance (or nerve) to act on them.
  • A scientist manqué — perhaps a natural thinker with a rigorous analytical mind who became a shopkeeper instead.

The possibilities are endless. Any unfulfilled vocation or identity can slot in.

Unlike in French, where adjectives change form based on gender, in English "manqué" is written the same way regardless of who it's describing — man, woman, or otherwise. You don't change the spelling. It stays "manqué" every time.
A Longer Example to Bring It All Together

Imagine a man named Harold. As a young person, Harold was obsessed with theatre. He memorized Shakespeare. He saw every play he could. His friends said he had a natural gift — extraordinary expressiveness, perfect comic timing. But his family had a hardware business that needed running, and so Harold stepped in, and ran it dutifully for forty years. He never once performed.

Yet even in the hardware store, Harold was theatrical. The way he told a story. The way he greeted customers like they were his audience. The dramatic pauses. The timing.

Harold is an actor manqué.

He never became the thing. But the thing is still visible in him. That is what "manqué" captures — and no other single word in English captures it quite as neatly.

[Noun] manqué = a person who had the nature, talent, or longing to be [noun], but never became it — and carries traces of that unlived identity.

It always follows its noun. Its tone is wistful rather than harsh. And it points not to a dramatic failure, but to a quieter, more human kind of loss: the life that was almost lived.
10367: A manservant is a man who is employed to personally serve another person, usually by working in or around that person's home. The word is simply a combination of "man" (male person) and "servant" (one who serves) — so it specifically means a male servant, as opposed to a female servant (called a maidservant, or simply a maid).
What "servant" means here

A servant is not just any hired worker. A servant works personally and closely for one specific person or household — handling tasks that keep the employer's everyday life comfortable and running smoothly. The employer of a manservant was typically addressed as the "master" (if male) or "mistress" (if female).
Who employed manservants?
Only wealthy people could afford them — aristocrats, noblemen, rich merchants, and gentlemen. Having one or more manservants was a sign of high social status.
What did a manservant actually do?

The duties of a manservant revolved around the personal comfort and daily needs of the employer:

  • Helping the master dress — laying out clothes, polishing shoes, fastening buttons
  • Looking after the master's wardrobe and personal belongings
  • Serving food and drinks at the table
  • Answering the door and receiving guests
  • Accompanying the master on journeys and travels
  • Running errands on behalf of the employer
  • Looking after horses and carriages

The defining feature is that the manservant worked close to the person, not at a distance (unlike, say, a farm laborer). His job was personal attendance.
The different types of manservants

"Manservant" is a broad, general word. Under this umbrella, there were many specific roles with their own titles:

  • Valet — a personal male attendant focused almost entirely on a gentleman's clothing, grooming, and personal care; the most intimate of manservants
  • Butler — the chief manservant of a household, who managed the other servants and oversaw the running of the entire house
  • Footman — a manservant who waited at table, answered the door, and carried things
  • Groom — a manservant who looked after the horses
  • Coachman — a manservant who drove the horse-drawn carriage

When someone simply says "my manservant," they often mean a personal male attendant in the style of a valet — someone attending to one person's daily needs.
Was a manservant a paid employee or a slave?

In most historical and literary contexts — particularly English literature from the 17th to 19th centuries — a manservant was a paid employee. He worked for wages and could, in principle, leave his employer. This is different from slavery.

However, in older texts — especially in the Bible (particularly the Old Testament in the King James Version) — the word "manservant" does sometimes refer to a male slave, reflecting the practice of slavery in the ancient world. So the meaning depends on the era and context of what you are reading.
Is the word still used today?

Not in everyday speech. "Manservant" sounds distinctly old-fashioned and formal in modern English. Today, people would more naturally say "valet," "butler," "personal attendant," or simply "servant."

You will, however, still encounter the word regularly in:

  • The Bible (especially the King James Version — it appears many times)
  • Classic English literature of the 17th, 18th, and 19th centuries
  • Historical fiction and period dramas (think: stories set in Victorian England)
  • Elevated or deliberate formal writing where an old-world tone is intended
The plural form — a common surprise

The plural of manservant is menservants, not "manservants." This is because the word contains "man," which pluralizes to "men" — just as in the words "workman → workmen" or "nobleman → noblemen." So: one manservant, several menservants.
Famous manservants in literature

The loyal, clever manservant is a beloved figure in classic fiction:

  • Jeeves, from P.G. Wodehouse's famous stories, is perhaps the most celebrated fictional manservant of all — a supremely intelligent valet who constantly saves his clueless employer, Bertie Wooster, from one disaster after another. His name has even entered the English language: calling someone "a real Jeeves" is a compliment meaning they are efficient, discreet, and quietly indispensable.
  • Passepartout, in Jules Verne's Around the World in Eighty Days, serves the English gentleman Phileas Fogg as his personal manservant throughout a globe-spanning adventure.
Example sentences

• The gentleman rang the bell, and his manservant appeared at the door within moments.
  • The household employed three manservants and five maids.
  • Jeeves was not just a manservant — he was, in every practical sense, the one who ran Bertie's life.
Summary in one sentence

A manservant is a man employed to personally and closely serve a wealthy employer — handling tasks like dressing, waiting at table, running errands, and attending to everyday needs — a figure common in history and classic literature, but largely replaced today by more specific job titles like valet or butler.
10368:
A mantel is the shelf — and sometimes the entire decorative frame — built around and above a fireplace.

Picture a fireplace in a living room. Right above the opening where the fire burns, there is usually a flat, horizontal ledge sticking out from the wall, like a shelf. That ledge is the mantel. It's a permanent, built-in part of the fireplace structure, not something you buy separately and place there.

Think of it this way: a fireplace has an opening (the hole where wood burns). The decorative structure that surrounds that opening — the two vertical columns on either side and the horizontal shelf across the top — is the mantel.

The shelf part is the most visible and useful portion. It can be made of wood, marble, stone, brick, or metal, depending on the home's style. In grand or traditional homes, mantels are heavily carved and ornate. In modern homes, they tend to be simple and clean.

The mantel shelf is prime decorating real estate. People place things on it: a clock, framed photos, candles, a painting or mirror hung above it, small sculptures, vases, or seasonal decorations. Because it sits right above the fireplace — a focal point of any room — whatever is placed on the mantel draws the eye naturally.

You'll often hear phrases like:

  • "She placed the old clock on the mantel."
  • "A family portrait hung just above the mantel."
  • "Christmas stockings were hung from the mantel."
The Full Structure vs. Just the Shelf

When people say "mantel," they sometimes mean only the shelf. Other times they mean the entire surround — the decorative framework including the sides, the shelf, and everything above it up to the ceiling. Context usually makes it clear.

You'll also encounter two closely related words:

  • Mantelpiece — essentially the same thing; often used to refer to the whole decorative structure around the fireplace, including the shelf.
  • Mantelshelf — specifically just the shelf portion, when you want to be precise.

All three words — mantel, mantelpiece, and mantelshelf — are used interchangeably in everyday life.
The All-Important Spelling Confusion: Mantel vs. Mantle

This is where many people go wrong, so pay close attention.

Mantel (ending in -el) = the fireplace shelf/structure. That's the word you're learning.

Mantle (ending in -le) = something completely different. A mantle is a loose, sleeveless cloak worn over clothing, like a cape. It also means a position of authority or responsibility that gets passed from one person to another (e.g., "She took on the mantle of leadership"). In science, the mantle is the thick layer of rock inside the Earth, between the outer crust and the core.

These two words are pronounced the same way and look almost identical, which is why writers mix them up all the time. If you're writing about a fireplace, always use mantel. If you're writing about a cloak, a role, or the Earth's interior, use mantle.

You'll mostly come across "mantel" in:

  • Interior design and home décor articles (how to style a mantel, what to put on a mantel)
  • Architecture writing (types of mantels, historical fireplace designs)
  • Fiction and literature (characters gathering around a fireplace, decorating a home, or noticing something placed above the fire)
  • Real estate listings (homes described as having "an original marble mantel")
Quick Mental Image to Lock It In

Imagine a classic English living room on a cold winter evening. A fire is crackling in the fireplace. Above the fire, resting on a wide stone shelf, is a ticking grandfather clock flanked by two brass candlesticks. That shelf — that entire framing structure — is the mantel. It is literally the "face" of the fireplace.
10369:
A mantelpiece is the decorative shelf — and often the entire decorative frame — that sits above and around a fireplace.

Think of it this way: a fireplace is just an opening in the wall where fire burns. A mantelpiece is everything built around and above that opening to make it look finished, elegant, and useful.
The two senses of the word

The word "mantelpiece" is used in two overlapping ways, and both are correct:

1. Just the shelf
In its most specific sense, a mantelpiece is the horizontal shelf that sticks out from the wall directly above the fireplace opening. It's a flat ledge, like a narrow table attached to the wall, sitting at roughly chest or eye level.

2. The whole structure around the fireplace
More broadly, "mantelpiece" can refer to the entire decorative surround — meaning the shelf plus the two vertical side panels (called jambs or legs) that frame the fireplace opening from left and right, and sometimes a decorative section above the shelf too. Think of it like a picture frame, but for a fireplace, with a shelf on top.

Both uses are widely understood. In everyday conversation, people most often mean the shelf when they say "mantelpiece."

A mantelpiece can be grand and ornate or simple and minimal, depending on the style of the home. It is usually made from:

  • Wood (the most common material, often painted white or left as natural wood)
  • Marble or stone (found in more formal, classical, or expensive homes)
  • Brick (in rustic or country-style homes)
  • Cast iron, tiles, or plaster (especially in older or Victorian-era homes)

The shelf itself is typically flat and wide enough to hold objects — usually anywhere from a few inches to a foot deep.

The mantelpiece has both a practical and a decorative purpose.

Practically, the shelf gives you a surface to place things on, positioned conveniently above the fireplace where it catches the eye.

Decoratively, it transforms the fireplace from a bare functional hole in the wall into a focal point — the visual centrepiece of a room. Rooms with a fireplace are often designed around it, with furniture arranged to face it.
What people put on a mantelpiece

The shelf of a mantelpiece is one of the most prominent display spots in a home. Common things placed there include:

  • A clock (the classic mantelpiece clock, placed at the centre)
  • Candles or candlesticks
  • Picture frames or family photographs
  • Vases with flowers
  • Figurines, sculptures, or ornaments
  • Mirrors hung on the wall above it (a very common pairing)
  • Christmas stockings hung from it during the festive season (a well-known tradition)

The mantelpiece is considered a place of honour in a home — items placed there are meant to be noticed and admired.

Originally, mantelpieces existed because fireplaces were the main source of heat. In modern homes, many fireplaces are decorative only (not actually used for heating), or are replaced by gas or electric fires. Yet mantelpieces remain extremely common as an architectural and interior design feature, because they give a room warmth, character, and a natural focal point — even when no fire is burning.

Some homes even install a mantelpiece with no fireplace at all — purely as a decorative feature on a wall, just for the look and the display shelf it provides.

• Mantel — a shorter form of "mantelpiece," used interchangeably; sometimes specifically refers to just the shelf
  • Mantelshelf — another word specifically for the shelf part
  • Chimneypiece — a more old-fashioned or formal word for the entire decorative structure around a fireplace
  • Overmantel — the decorative section above the mantelpiece shelf, often featuring a mirror, carved panels, or artwork

• She placed a framed photograph on the mantelpiece.
  • The old house had a beautiful marble mantelpiece in the sitting room.
  • He hung his Christmas stocking from the mantelpiece.
  • The mantelpiece was the grandest feature of the entire room.

In short: a mantelpiece is the shelf and decorative surround above a fireplace — a structural feature of a room that is both useful as a display surface and important as a design element that draws the eye and gives the space its character.
